title: E-GEO: A Testbed for Generative Engine Optimization in E-Commerce
claim: A rewriter modifies one item before the same fixed ranker, and the resulting rank gain is the optimization objective.
layout: Top engine pipeline, bottom rewrite loop; right-hand before/after ranked lists joined by a +3 arrow
description: A flow diagram with two stages. The top band is a grey rounded box labeled Generative Engine / Shopping Agent. It holds boxes for User Query (with a speech-bubble example), Retrieval from the product catalog, Candidate Listing of Products A–E, an LLM Re-ranker in blue, and a Response of ranked products, joined by arrows. Below it, a red box holds the original Product E listing and feeds a large orange GEO Rewriter with a gear icon. That produces a green rewritten Product E listing. Each listing goes through its own blue LLM Re-ranker. On the right, a Before Rewriting list puts Product E at rank 4, highlighted red. An After Rewriting list puts it at rank 1, highlighted green. An orange +3 ranks bubble links the two lists and points back to the rewriter, labeled Optimizable, with the constraints no access to user queries and rewrites remain factual. The eye goes first to the orange rewriter and the colored rank lists.
caption: GEO in e-commerce. Top: the generative engine retrieves a short candidate listing from the product catalog for a user query; an LLM re-ranker orders the candidates, and the engine returns a ranked list of recommended products. Bottom: a GEO rewriter rewrites one target listing (Product E), and the same re-ranker orders the same candidates again. The resulting rank improvement is the objective the rewriter optimizes, without access to user queries and constrained to remain factual.
abstract: With the rise of large language models (LLMs), generative engines have become powerful alternatives to traditional search, creating the need for generative engine optimization (GEO)---improving content visibility and relevance for generative engines. Despite its growing importance, current GEO practices are largely ad hoc, and their impacts remain understudied. In e-commerce, for instance, conversational shopping agents now guide consumers to relevant products, yet it is unclear if GEO can affect how products surface to users. We address this gap by introducing E-GEO, which contains 13,746 realistic, multi-sentence consumer product queries, each paired with 10 retrieved Amazon listings, capturing rich intent, constraints, preferences, and shopping contexts that existing datasets miss. Using this dataset, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of e-commerce GEO across five representative generative engines, seven LLM rewriters, and fifteen rewriting heuristics. We further formulate GEO as an optimization problem and develop a prompt meta-optimization algorithm that significantly improves over heuristic baselines. Notably, prompts independently optimized from different heuristics converge to a stable pattern, suggesting a shared, transferable GEO strategy. Finally, we red-team the GEO system through both static and optimization-based attacks and show that, under a simple in-prompt defense in our setting, gains from GEO reflect genuine content improvement, anchoring GEO as a substantive optimization problem.
